The TypeScript compiler has reported zero errors after several runs (`bunx tsc --noEmit`), confirming that the code is syntactically correct and the types line up. However, static analysis alone isn’t enough—I need to verify the runtime behavior of the TUI, especially the new hint handling and the overall UI flow. The best way to do that is to actually launch the application in a terminal emulator that can render Ink components, capture the output, and inspect the first few lines to see that the UI renders as expected (e.g., the command palette, the approval component, any initial messages).

Running the TUI directly in the current shell would interfere with my own interaction and would be hard to capture programmatically. Using `tmux` is a common pattern for headless UI testing: I can start a detached session, run the app inside it, let it render for a few seconds, then capture the pane contents. This gives me a clean, reproducible snapshot of the UI without manual intervention.

I need to be careful to clean up any previous test session that might already exist, to avoid “session already exists” errors. So I’ll prepend a `tmux kill-session -t glint` (silencing any errors with `2>/dev/null`). Then I’ll create a new detached session named `glint` with a reasonable size (`-x 100 -y 30`) and set its working directory to a temporary location (`/tmp/glint-test`). Inside that session I’ll run the TUI entry point: `bun run /home/lane/GR/glint-cli/src/index.tsx --no-intro`. The `--no-intro` flag skips the introductory splash that would otherwise dominate the first lines, letting me focus on the core UI. I’ll also redirect any stderr output to a temporary log file (`/tmp/glint-tui-err.log`) so I can inspect errors later if needed.

After starting the session, I should give the app a moment to initialize and render. A short `sleep 3` should be sufficient. Then I’ll capture the pane’s contents with `tmux capture-pane -t glint -p`, pipe it to `head -25` to limit the output to the first 25 lines (enough to see the initial UI elements without overwhelming the console). This command will return the captured text as the tool’s output, which I can then examine for correctness.

All of this can be expressed in a single Bash tool call. The command string will be:

```
tmux kill-session -t glint 2>/dev/null; \
tmux new-session -d -s glint -x 100 -y 30 -c /tmp/glint-test \
  'bun run /home/lane/GR/glint-cli/src/index.tsx --no-intro 2>/tmp/glint-tui-err.log' \
&& sleep 3 && tmux capture-pane -t glint -p | head -25
```
